evidence.quote:
He was oppressed by the weight and the
torment of this thing called life, and still more was he
oppressed by the fear of death.
evidence.paraphrase: Old Ebbits is described as weary of life and fearful of death.

evidence.quote:
But the white man speaks true in different
ways.	a To-day he speaks true one way, to-morrow he speaks
true another way, and there is no understanding him nor his
way.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits contrasts the inconsistent behavior of the white man with a consistency the Indian expects.

evidence.quote:
Always does the Indian do the one thing in the one way.	a Always
does the moose come down from the high mountains when the winter
is here.	a Always does the salmon come in the spring when the
ice has gone out of the river.	a Always does everything do
all things in the same way, and the Indian knows and
understands.	a But the white man does not do all things in
the same way, and the Indian does not know nor understand.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits contrasts the predictability of nature and Indian custom with the unpredictability of the white man.

evidence.quote:
But the white man!	a When his mouth is full with the juice,
what does he do?	a That juice, that juice of great value, he
spits it out in the snow and it is lost.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator's culture chews and swallows tobacco juice, while the white man spits it out, from Ebbits's perspective a foolish waste.

evidence.quote:
When man takes your meat, or your
canoe, or your wife, you kill that man.	a That is the law,
and it is a good law.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits describes the Indian law that a thief must be killed, contrasting it with white man's treatment.

evidence.quote:
He has a
house.	a He puts Mobits in that house.	a The roof is
good.	a The walls are thick.	a He makes a fire that
Mobits may be warm.	a He gives Mobits plenty grub to
eat.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits describes imprisonment as the white man feeding and sheltering a thief rather than punishing him, which he finds baffling.

evidence.quote:
Ai! ai!	a wailed Zilla.	a 	Crafty and
wise was he, and my first-born!
evidence.paraphrase: Zilla wails in grief over the death of her first-born son Moklan.

evidence.quote:
if you have in thy country bad hunting, or bad water, you must
make payment.	a It is just.	a It is the law.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits explains the customary law that compensation must be paid for deaths caused by bad hunting or dangerous water.

evidence.quote:
All the
way do they take him down the river to the end, where it runs
into a lake which is larger than all the land and large as the
sky.
evidence.paraphrase: Yamikan is taken far down the river to a lake (the sea) larger than all the land, a place beyond the village's experience.

evidence.quote:
Also, it is made of iron, this boat, and yet does it not
sink.	a This I do not understand
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits marvels that the white man's iron boat does not sink, something beyond his understanding.

evidence.quote:
a land where there is no snow.	a I cannot believe
this.	a It is not in the nature of things that when winter
comes there shall be no snow.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits struggles to believe there is a land (California) where no snow ever falls, contrasting with his own world.

evidence.quote:
I have heard the name
before, but I would hear it again, if it be the same	a thus
will I know if I have heard lies or true talk.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits seeks to verify the name of the snowless country by cross-checking it to determine whether he was told the truth.

evidence.quote:
All the time does he seek after bugs and
flies.	a He does not eat the bugs and flies, then why does he
seek after them?
evidence.paraphrase: A visiting white man collects insects, eggshells, bird skins, and old bones, which Ebbits describes as incomprehensible scientific collecting.

evidence.quote:
He takes
Bidarshik to Cambell Fort, and he ties a rope around his neck,
so, and, when his feet are no more on the ground, he
dies.
evidence.paraphrase: Unlike Yamikan, Bidarshik is hanged for killing a white man, leaving Ebbits without sons.

evidence.quote:
Go forth,	a I say,
	and find a white man, and, even as Yamikan, do you kill
that white man.	a Then will the soldier white men come and
get you, and even as they took Yamikan will they take you across
the salt lake to the white man's land.
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits, reasoning from Yamikan's earlier outcome, advises his son to kill a white man expecting the same reward, but the outcome differs.

evidence.quote:
How was I to know the way of the white man is never
twice the same?
evidence.paraphrase: Ebbits laments that the white man's behavior changes from day to day, making it impossible to predict.
